questions.prompt: Complete: "My brother usually ___ to school by bus."
questions.explanation: "usually" marks a habit, so we use the present simple; with the third-person singular subject "my brother" the verb takes -s: goes. "go" forgets the -s; "is going" is the present continuous (action now), which clashes with "usually"; "going" alone is not a finite verb.

options.text: She is wanting a new bike.
She is want a new bike.

questions.explanation: "want" is a stative verb (a wish, not an action), so it stays in the present simple, and "she" adds -s: she wants a new bike. "is wanting" puts a stative verb in the continuous; "She want" forgets the -s of he/she/it; "is want" mixes "be" with a base verb.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Look! It ___ outside, so take an umbrella."
questions.explanation: "Look!" shows the action is happening at this moment, so we use the present continuous; "it" takes "is": it is raining. "are" goes only with a plural subject; "rains" is present simple (a habit or general truth); "rain" lacks both the -s and the continuous form.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct question about your sister:
questions.explanation: Present simple questions with he/she/it use the auxiliary "does" + the base verb: Does your sister speak English? "does" already carries the -s, so "Does … speaks" marks it twice; "Do" is for I/you/we/they; "Is … speak" mixes "be" with a base verb.

questions.prompt: Complete: "My father usually works in an office, but this week he ___ from home."
questions.explanation: "usually" gives the habit (the office), and "this week" marks a temporary situation around now, different from that habit, so we use the present continuous; "he" takes "is": is working. "works" (present simple) would make working from home his normal routine, which contradicts "usually works in an office"; "work" forgets the -s; "are" goes only with a plural subject.

In the present simple negative with he, the auxiliary "does" carries the -s and the main verb stays in its base form: he doesn't understand. "don't" is the wrong auxiliary for "he"; "doesn't understands" double-marks the -s; "isn't understand" mixes "be" with a base verb.
